newsitem.title: USA: U.S. land chief Dombeck to lead Forest Service.
newsitem.headline: U.S. land chief Dombeck to lead Forest Service.

text.p: Mike Dombeck, the land management director for the Interior Department, was named on Friday as U.S. Forest Service chief, and said he hoped to build a consensus among opposing groups regarding land use.

Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman, in announcing the appointment, referred to Dombeck as a "unifying figure" and said his tenure should be marked by better relations with Congress over operation of the 191 million-acre national forest system.

Dombeck stressed a desire to build consensus and deflected questions about his policy plans. "Our biggest challenge is to bring people together on the land," he told a news conference. "If the land is in good shape, everybody benefits."

As Forest Service chief, Dombeck must balance the interests of loggers, conservationists and recreation users. There have been fights for several years over how to preserve rare plants and animals while allowing other uses of the forests.

Timber harvest on federal land has dropped to about four billion board feet a year, compared to more than 10 billion during the late 1980s. A board foot is equal to a lumber board one-foot-square and one-inch thick.
The decline in timber harvesting was due to court rulings and steps to save endangered species in the Northwest.
Since February 1994, Dombeck has been acting director of the Bureau of Land Management at the Interior Department, where he oversaw 264 million acres of public land.

He began his career with the federal government in 1978 as a Forest Service fishery biologist in Milwaukee and was the agency's national fisheries program manager in 1989 when he shifted to Interior. Dombeck, 48, is a Wisconsin native.
The Wilderness Society environmental group said Dombeck was qualified to be a "first-rate Forest Service chief" and would protect the forests.
"We're pleased that the habit of selecting timber people has been broken," said Bill Meadows, the society's president.

Alaska Republican Frank Murkowski, who chairs the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, said he would work with Dombeck but was disappointed the chief was not drawn from within the agency. He called Dombeck "the second politically appointed chief" and the first from outside the agency.
Glickman said Dombeck's appointment did not represent a politicization of land management. "We have many, many, many people in the Forest Service who worked elsewhere," he said.
Dombeck succeeds Jack Ward Thomas, who announced in October that he was retiring and would become a university instructor.
